claim: The primary vibrissae motor cortex (vM1) is responsible for generating whisking movements.
source: The primary vibrissae motor cortex (vM1) is responsible for generating whisking movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: vM1 sends information directly to the sensory barrel cortex (vS1).
source: In parallel, vM1 also sends information directly to the sensory barrel cortex (vS1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Optogenetic activation of vM1 supra-linearly amplified the response of vS1 neurons to passive vibrissa stimulation in all cortical layers measured.
source: Optogenetic activation of vM1 supra-linearly amplified the response of vS1 neurons to passive vibrissa stimulation in all cortical layers measured.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3, showing measurements across different cortical layers.

claim: Maximal amplification occurred when onset of vM1 optogenetic activation preceded vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms.
source: Maximal amplification occurred when onset of vM1 optogenetic activation preceded vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, which tests different time delays between vM1 activation and vibrissa stimulation.

claim: vM1 activation sharpened angular tuning of vS1 neurons in all cortical layers measured.
source: In addition to amplification, vM1 activation also sharpened angular tuning of vS1 neurons in all cortical layers measured.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6, showing angular tuning measurements across cortical layers.

claim: vM1 sends preparatory signals to vS1 that serve to amplify and sharpen the response of neurons in the barrel cortex to incoming sensory input signals.
source: Our findings indicated that in addition to output motor signals, vM1 also sends preparatory signals to vS1 that serve to amplify and sharpen the response of neurons in the barrel cortex to incoming sensory input signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, particularly the temporal relationship showing maximal effect when vM1 activation precedes vibrissa stimulation.

claim: Rodents are equipped with an array of vibrissae on their snout (mystacial vibrissae) that serve as a highly developed tactile somatosensory organ.
source: Rodents are equipped with an array of vibrissae on their snout (mystacial vibrissae) that serve as a highly developed tactile somatosensory organ (Woolsey and Van der Loos, 1970; Carvell and Simons, 1990; Petersen, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008; Diamond and Arabzadeh, 2013; Feldmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rodents typically produce whisking movements of their vibrissae to probe their environment and palpate objects located within the vibrissae reach.
source: To probe their environment, rodents typically produce whisking movements of their vibrissae, and palpate objects located within the vibrissae reach.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rodent behavior.

claim: Physical contact between external objects and vibrissae generate forces and vibrations at the base of the vibrissae, which are sensed by specialized mechanoreceptors located at the vibrissae pad.
source: The physical contact between external objects and vibrissae generate forces and vibrations at the base of the vibrissae, which are sensed by specialized mechanoreceptors located at the vibrissae pad.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanosensory mechanism of vibrissae.

claim: Sensory information collected by mechanoreceptors is conveyed to the cortex via the VPM and PoM nuclei of the thalamus.
source: In turn, the sensory information collected by these mechanoreceptors is conveyed to the cortex via the VPM and PoM nuclei of the thalamus (Petersen, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The main cortical region receiving sensory information from the vibrissae is the somatosensory S1 barrel cortex (vS1), which is arranged somatotopically, with each vibrissa represented by a separate and discrete barrel-like region.
source: The main cortical region receiving sensory information from the vibrissae is the somatosensory S1 barrel cortex (vS1), which is arranged somatotopically, with each vibrissa represented by a separate and discrete barrel-like region (Izraeli and Porter, 1995; Petersen, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008; Bosman et al., 2011; Diamond and Arabzadeh, 2013; Feldmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The vibrissae-barrel somatosensory system typically uses active sensing.
source: The vibrissae-barrel somatosensory system typically uses active sensing (Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Schroeder et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Whisking movements are evoked by descending commands from the primary vibrissae motor cortex (vM1).
source: Whisking movements are evoked by descending commands from the primary vibrissae motor cortex (vM1) (Grinevich et al., 2005; Gerdjikov et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2011; Petersen, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It is still unclear whether neurons in vM1 directly drive the facial nucleus, or alternatively activate a central pattern generator (CPG) in the brainstem that in turn rhythmically drives the facial nucleus.
source: It is still unclear whether neurons in vM1 directly drive the facial nucleus, or alternatively activate a central pattern generator (CPG) in the brainstem that in turn rhythmically drives the facial nucleus (Grinevich et al., 2005; Kleinfeld et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2014; Petersen, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: vM1 directly sends information to other structures in the sensory-motor vibrissae-barrel loop, especially the vS1 barrel cortex.
source: In addition to the descending output motor information to the brain stem, vM1 also directly sends information to other structures in the sensory-motor vibrissae-barrel loop, and especially the vS1 barrel cortex (Aronoff et al., 2010; Veinante and Deschênes, 2003; Mao et al., 2011; Feldmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The direct vM1 to vS1 pathway originates mostly from layer 2–3 and layer 5A pyramidal neurons in vM1 and terminates mostly on layer 5 neurons and to a lesser degree layer 2–3 neurons of vS1.
source: This direct vM1 to vS1 pathway originates mostly from layer 2–3 and layer 5A pyramidal neurons in vM1 and terminates mostly on layer 5 neurons and to a lesser degree layer 2–3 neurons of vS1 (Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: vM1 inputs to vS1 carry information regarding both motor parameters of whisking, as well as more complex sensory information.
source: Previous functional studies have shown that vM1 inputs to vS1 carry information regarding both motor parameters of whisking, as well as more complex sensory information (Petreanu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Inputs from vM1 have been shown to modify the network state of the vS1 barrel cortex, and increase the coding reliability of complex sensory stimuli in vS1.
source: Moreover, inputs from vM1 have been shown to modify the network state of the vS1 barrel cortex, and increase the coding reliability of complex sensory stimuli in vS1 (Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The vibrissae-barrel system functions as a motor-sensory loop.
source: A major obstacle we encountered in tackling this question was the fact the vibrissae-barrel system functions as a motor-sensory loop (Kleinfeld et al., 1999; Diamond et al., 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: vM1 can influence vS1 neurons both directly and indirectly.
source: For example, vM1 activation can affect vS1 neuron both via direct inputs connecting the two areas and indirectly via whisking-evoked stimulation of mechanoreceptors in the vibrissae pad.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known anatomy and physiology of the system.

claim: The buccolabialis branch of the facial nerve was cut to eliminate cortical-driven whisking movements in all experiments.
source: In all our experiments, we cut the buccolabialis branch of the facial nerve to eliminate cortical-driven whisking movements.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The principal barrel was identified prior to electrode insertion using intrinsic imaging.
source: The principal barrel was identified prior to electrode insertion using intrinsic imaging (for details see Garion et al., 2014), and verified by manual deflection of vibrissae during extracellular multi-unit recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: 200 ms passive ramp and hold vibrissa deflection evoked short on and off responses.
source: Typically, the 200 ms passive ramp and hold vibrissa deflection-evoked short on and off responses (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 84% of all recorded neurons in vM1 significantly increased their firing rate during 20 ms 473 nm laser pulses.
source: Overall 84% of all recorded neurons in vM1 significantly increased their firing rate during 20 ms 473 nm laser pulses (109 vM1 neurons from five rats).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in vM1.

claim: vM1 neurons increased their average firing by 563% ± 84% during the laser pulse time.
source: On average vM1 neurons increased their average firing by 563% ± 84% during the pulse time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in vM1.

claim: The average latency between laser onset and increased firing in vM1 was 4.81 ± 0.43 ms.
source: Moreover, the average latency between laser onset and increased firing in vM1 was 4.81 ± 0.43 ms (mean ± SEM, 109 neurons from five rats), with 41% of neurons showing a unimodal response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in vM1.

claim: 41% of vM1 neurons showed a unimodal response to optogenetic stimulation.
source: Moreover, the average latency between laser onset and increased firing in vM1 was 4.81 ± 0.43 ms (mean ± SEM, 109 neurons from five rats), with 41% of neurons showing a unimodal response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings in vM1.

claim: The magnitude of the responses recorded in vS1 neurons depended on the duration of the laser pulse, and gradually increased as the duration of the laser pulse increased from 5 to 20 ms.
source: The magnitude of the responses recorded in vS1 neurons depended on the duration of the laser pulse, and gradually increased as the duration of the laser pulse increased from 5 to 20 ms (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: During the on response, paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation were significantly larger (by an average of 39%) than the expected linear sum of the two stimuli applied separately.
source: During the on response, paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation were significantly larger (by an average of 39%) than the expected linear sum of the two stimuli applied separately (Figure 2A, 237 neurons from seven rats).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In multi-unit analysis, the on response to paired ramp and hold vibrissa deflection and optogenetic vM1 stimulation was 34% larger than the expected sum of the two stimuli applied separately.
source: In the case of multi-unit analysis the on response to paired ramp and hold vibrissa deflection and optogenetic vM1 stimulation was 34% larger than the expected sum of the two stimuli applied separately.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multi-unit analysis.

claim: In 57% of individual neurons (135 out of 237 neurons) paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation was significantly larger than the expected sum of solitary vibrissa deflection and vM1 optogenetic activation.
source: Moreover, we found that in 57% of individual neurons (135 out of 237 neurons) paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation was significantly larger than the expected sum of solitary vibrissa deflection and vM1 optogenetic activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-unit analysis.

claim: A small yet significant supra-linearity was also observed during the off response despite the fact that the 20 ms optogenetic stimulation was applied at the onset of the 200 ms ramp and hold vibrissa deflection.
source: Interestingly, a small yet significant supra-linearity was also observed during the off response despite the fact we applied the 20 ms optogenetic stimulation at the onset of the 200 ms ramp and hold vibrissa deflection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Paired vM1-vibrissa deflection stimulation yielded an average off response that was 15% larger than the expected sum of the two stimuli applied separately.
source: Paired vM1-vibrissa deflection stimulation yielded an average off response that was 15% larger than the expected sum of the two stimuli applied separately (expected average linear sum of 207.6% ± 11.7% compared to 238% ± 12.4% of the averaged measured paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation, p<0.05, 237 units from seven rats).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Putative layers 2–3 were defined as extending up to 600 µm from the pia, layer 4 as extending 650–800 µm from the pia, and layer 5 as extending beyond 800 µm from the pia.
source: We defined putative layers 2–3 as extending up to 600 µm from the pia, layer 4 as extending 650–800 µm from the pia, and layer 5 as extending beyond 800 µm from the pia.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for layer assignment.

claim: Cortical layers were determined solely by the distance of the recording contact from the cortical surface, as cortical layers could not be verified by histological criteria.
source: It is important to stress that cortical layers were determined solely by the distance of the recording contact from the cortical surface, as we could not verify cortical layers by histological criteria.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Paired opto-stimulation of vM1 supra-linearly amplified the on response of vS1 neurons to ramp and hold vibrissa deflection in all cortical layers recorded.
source: Paired opto-stimulation of vM1 supra-linearly amplified the on response vS1 neurons to ramp and hold vibrissa deflection in all cortical layers recorded.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Supra-linearity was largest in putative layers 2–3 and 5, and smallest in putative layer 4 neurons.
source: Supra-linearity was largest in putative layers 2–3 and 5, and smallest in putative layer 4 neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No significant differences were observed between layers 2–3 and 5 in supra-linearity.
source: No significant differences were observed between layers 2–3 and 5 (Figure 2D, analysis for the different layers is shown for the on response).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The response evoked by paired vM1 optogenetic activation with artificial whisking against sandpaper was 42% larger than the expected linear sum of the two individual responses applied separately.
source: On average, the response evoked by paired vM1 optogenetic activation with artificial whisking against sandpaper was 42% larger than the expected linear sum of the two individual responses applied separately (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: 69% of neurons (164 out of 241 neurons) had measured paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation that were significantly larger than the expected linear sum of isolated vibrissa deflection and vM1 optogenetic activation in artificial whisking experiments.
source: When we calculated the ratio of the measured versus expected responses for individual neurons we found that 69% of neurons (164 out of 241 neurons) had measured paired vM1-vibrissa stimulation that were significantly larger than the expected linear sum of isolated vibrissa deflection and vM1 optogenetic activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from artificial whisking experiments.

claim: Pairing vM1 activation with artificial whisking supra-linearly amplified the response in all recorded neocortical layers.
source: Similar to ramp and hold vibrissa stimulation, pairing vM1 activation with artificial whisking supra-linearly amplified the response in all recorded neocortical layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When vM1 was optogenetically activated 0–50 ms prior to passive vibrissa stimulation the paired response was significantly larger than that evoked by isolated passive vibrissa stimulation.
source: When vM1 was optogenetically activated 0–50 ms prior to passive vibrissa stimulation the paired response was significantly larger than that evoked by isolated passive vibrissa stimulation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When vM1 was activated 75–100 ms before or 20–50 ms after passive vibrissa stimulation the combined response did not significantly differ from the isolated vibrissa stimulation.
source: In contrast, when vM1 was activated 75–100 ms before or 20–50 ms after passive vibrissa stimulation the combined response did not significantly differ from the isolated vibrissa stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The largest facilitating effect of vM1 activation was observed when the onset of the optogenetic vM1 activation preceded the onset of vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms.
source: The largest facilitating effect of vM1 activation was observed when the onset of the optogenetic vM1 activation preceded the onset of vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The temporal relationship showing maximal effect at -20 ms was observed for both ramp and hold vibrissa deflection and artificial whisking against sandpaper.
source: These findings were observed for both ramp and hold vibrissa deflection and artificial whisking against sandpaper (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex show a preference for the direction in which the vibrissa is deflected (angular tuning).
source: Previous studies have reported that neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex show a preference for the direction in which the vibrissa is deflected (angular tuning) (Bruno et al., 2003; Andermann and Moore, 2006; Kremer et al., 2011; Lavzin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Angular tuning in neurons is located in layers 2–3 and layer 4.
source: Consistent with previous results, we found that angular tuning in neurons is located in layers 2–3 and layer 4 (Bruno et al., 2003; Andermann and Moore, 2006; Kremer et al., 2011; Lavzin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is consistent with previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: Layer 5 neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex also show similar angular tuning.
source: We further found that layer 5 neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex also show similar angular tuning.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the experimental data.

claim: 62% ± 8% of all recorded neurons showed significant angular tuning, with no significant differences between putative layers.
source: We quantified the percent of neurons with significant angular tuning, and found that 62% ± 8% of all recorded neurons showed significant angular tuning, with no significant differences between putative layers (significant angular tuning was defined by significant difference at the 0.05 level for comparison of the responses to the preferred angle and to the three least preferred angles).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from angular tuning experiments.

claim: Paired vM1 optogenetic activation significantly increased the average SI for angular tuning in vS1 barrel cortex neurons.
source: In these experiments, we found that paired vM1 optogenetic activation significantly increased the average SI for angular tuning in vS1 barrel cortex neurons (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Paired vM1 optogenetic activation resulted in a right shift of the SI value histogram.
source: which resulted from a right shift of the SI value histogram by vM1 activation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A significant increase in the SI of the preferred direction was observed in both 50–60 day old and 90–100 day old rats.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in the SI of the preferred direction in both 50–60 day old and 90–100 day old rats (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: While the SI of the preferred direction increased, the SI values of the worst three angular directions decreased by vM1 activation, although this reduction did not reach statistical significance.
source: Furthermore, as expected, while the SI of the preferred direction increased, the SI values of the worst three angular directions decreased by vM1 activation, although this reduction did not reach statistical significance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In many cases the activation of vM1 increased the absolute response to the worst angles.
source: It is important to stress that although the SI to the worst directions decreased, in many cases the activation of vM1 increased the absolute response to the worst angles (see examples in Figure 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multi-unit activity demonstrated that vM1 optogenetic activation significantly sharpened angular tuning of vS1 neurons.
source: Similar to single- unit activity multi-unit activity, again demonstrated that vM1 optogenetic activation significantly sharpened angular tuning of vS1 neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The sharpening of angular tuning with multi-unit analysis is consistent with the previously reported spatial mapping of angular tuning in the barrel cortex.
source: The fact we observed sharpening of angular tuning with multi-unit analysis is consistent with the previously reported spatial mapping of angular tuning in the barrel cortex (Kremer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: vM1 optogenetic activation significantly increased the amplitude of the vector sum.
source: We found that similar to the effect on SI, vM1 optogenetic activation significantly increased the amplitude of the vector sum (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The amplitude of the vector sum increased by 29% ± 7% on average.
source: On average, the amplitude of the vector sum increased by 29% ± 7%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: A significant sharpening of angular tuning by paired vM1 activation was observed in all recorded neocortical layers (layers 2–5), with no significant differences between the recorded putative layers.
source: A significant sharpening of angular tuning by paired vM1 activation was observed in all recorded neocortical layers (layers 2–5), with no significant differences between the recorded putative layers (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The majority of neurons retained their preferred angular direction during opto-stimulation of vM1.
source: The majority of neurons retained their preferred angular direction during opto-stimulation of vM1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The probability for retaining the preferred angular direction during paired vM1 activation was larger in neurons with higher SI during solitary unpaired vibrissa stimulation, with 70.9% of neurons with SI greater than two retaining their preferred angular direction after paired vM1 activation.
source: The probability for retaining the preferred angular direction during paired vM1 activation was larger in neurons with higher SI during solitary unpaired vibrissa stimulation, with 70.9% of neurons with SI greater than two retaining their preferred angular direction after paired vM1 activation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Neurons that retained their preferred angular direction showed a significantly greater degree of sharpening of their angular tuning curve by vM1 optogenetic activation, as compared to neurons that changed their preferred angular tuning during paired vM1 activation.
source: Moreover, neurons that retained their preferred angular direction showed a significantly greater degree of sharpening of their angular tuning curve by vM1 optogenetic activation, as compared to neurons that changed their preferred angular tuning during paired vM1 activation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The strongest monosynaptic connections between vM1 and vS1 exist between neurons in layers 2–3 and layer 5A of vM1 and layer 5A and 5B neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex.
source: The strongest monosynaptic connections between vM1 and vS1 exist between neurons in layers 2–3 and layer 5A of vM1 and layer 5A and 5B neurons in the vS1 barrel cortex (Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Reciprocal connections exist between layers 2–3 and 5A neurons in vS1 and vM1 neurons.
source: Interestingly, reciprocal connections also exist between layers 2–3 and 5A neurons in vS1 and vM1 neurons (Hooks et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A subset of vM1 axons reach layer 1 of the vS1 barrel cortex, and carry both motor information regarding different vibrissa movement parameters and more complex sensory information regarding contact of vibrissae with objects, and spatial localization of objects.
source: A subset of vM1 axons reach layer 1 of the vS1 barrel cortex, and carry both motor information regarding different vibrissa movement parameters and more complex sensory information regarding contact of vibrissae with objects, and spatial localization of objects (Petreanu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: vM1 inputs innervating tuft dendrites of vS1 layer 5 pyramidal neurons critically participate in dendritic spike initiation when vibrissae actively touched objects in a location and angle-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, vM1 inputs innervating tuft dendrites of vS1 layer 5 pyramidal neurons critically participate in dendritic spike initiation when vibrissae actively touched objects in a location and angle-dependent manner (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Short (20 ms) optogenetic stimulation of vM1 neurons significantly increased firing of vS1 barrel neurons.
source: In this study, we show that short (20 ms) optogenetic stimulation of vM1 neurons significantly increased firing of vS1 barrel neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The findings are in agreement with the results of a recent study performed in awake behaving rodents that reported activation of vS1 barrel neurons by optogenetic stimulation of vM1 neurons.
source: These findings are in agreement with the results of a recent study performed in awake behaving rodents that reported activation of vS1 barrel neurons by optogenetic stimulation of vM1 neurons (Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Zagha et al. (2013) reported that optogenetic activation of vM1 resulted in context-dependent changes in the network state of the barrel cortex and increased reliability of responses to complex sensory stimuli.
source: Moreover, Zagha et al. (2013) also reported that optogenetic activation of vM1 resulted in context-dependent changes in the network state of the barrel cortex and increased reliability of responses to complex sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Motor information from vM1 neurons and sensory information from the vibrissae summate supra-linearly in vS1 barrel neurons.
source: First, we show that motor information from vM1 neurons and sensory information from the vibrissae summate supra-linearly in vS1 barrel neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Maximal vM1-vibrissa interactions occurred when vM1 activation preceded vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms.
source: We found maximal vM1-vibrissa interactions occurred when vM1 activation preceded vibrissa stimulation by 20 ms.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The optimal temporal window for vM1-vibrissa input interactions suggested that vM1 sent primarily feedforward information regarding the planned vibrissa movements, rather than feedback information originating in the sensory motor loop.
source: This optimal temporal window for vM1-vibrissa input interactions suggested that vM1 sent primarily feedforward information regarding the planned vibrissa movements, rather than feedback information originating in the sensory motor loop.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: vM1 activation not only amplified the response of vS1 barrel neurons to incoming vibrissa sensory inputs, but also sharpened their angular tuning curve.
source: Finally, we show that vM1 activation, not only amplified the response of vS1 barrel neurons to incoming vibrissa sensory inputs, but also sharpened their angular tuning curve.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: vM1 inputs participated in increasing both the sensitivity and specificity of barrel cortex neurons to incoming sensory information from the vibrissae.
source: Taken together, it seems vM1 inputs participated in increasing both the sensitivity and specificity of barrel cortex neurons to incoming sensory information from the vibrissae.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The direct effect of vM1 on vS1 neurons may underlie the difference between passive and active sensing in the barrel vibrissa somatosensory system.
source: The direct effect of vM1 on vS1 neurons may underlie the difference between passive and active sensing in the barrel vibrissa somatosensory system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Dendrites of neocortical excitatory neurons can support generation of local dendritic sodium, calcium and NMDA spikes.
source: Previous studies have shown that dendrites of neocortical excitatory neurons can support generation of local dendritic sodium, calcium and NMDA spikes (Stuart et al., 1997; Larkum et al., 1999, 2009; Schiller et al., 2000; Polsky et al., 2004; London and Häusser, 2005; Branco et al., 2010; Lavzin et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Harnett et al., 2013; Major et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2014; Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is possible that pairing vM1 inputs with inputs carrying vibrissa sensory information results in initiation of local dendritic spikes in vS1 neurons.
source: It is possible that pairing vM1 inputs with inputs carrying vibrissa sensory information results in initiation of local dendritic spikes vS1 neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Several previous in vivo studies reported initiation of dendritic spikes in tuft dendrites of vS1 layer-5 pyramidal neurons in response to vM1 and M2 activation.
source: Consistent with this possibility are the results of several previous in vivo studies that reported initiation of dendritic spikes in tuft dendrites of vS1 layer-5 pyramidal neurons in response to vM1 and M2 activation (Xu et al., 2012; Manita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: vM1 inputs may selectively innervate VIP inhibitory inter neurons, as described for the medial prefrontal inputs to the auditory cortex.
source: For example, vM1 inputs may selectively innervate VIP inhibitory inter neurons, as described for the medial prefrontal inputs to the auditory cortex (Lee et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogous findings in another system, supported by citations.

claim: In the case where vM1 inputs activate VIP inter neurons, vM1 inputs will activate VIP inter neurons, which will inhibit other inhibitory inter neurons, and in turn secondary excite pyramidal neurons in vS1.
source: In this case, vM1 inputs will activate VIP inter neurons, which will inhibit other inhibitory inter neurons, and in turn secondary excite pyramidal neurons in vS1.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: The barrel vibrissa system uses active sensing to palpate objects in the near vicinity of the rodents head.
source: The barrel vibrissa system uses active sensing to palpate objects in the near vicinity of the rodents head.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: vM1, the motor cortex of the barrel vibrissa system, is responsible for generating the whisking movements of the mystacial vibrissae.
source: Typically, vM1, the motor cortex of the barrel vibrissa system, is responsible for generating the whisking movements of the mystacial vibrissae.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: vM1 can drive whisking either by directly activating lower motor neurons in the facial nucleus, especially during protraction movements, or alternatively, by activating a brain stem CPG located in close proximity to or within the Botzinger complex.
source: vM1 can drive whisking either by directly activating lower motor neurons in the facial nucleus, especially during protraction movements, or alternatively, by activating a brain stem CPG located in close proximity to or within the Botzinger complex. In the latter case the CPG drives the facial nucleus to generate rhythmic movements (Grinevich et al., 2005; Haiss and Schwarz, 2005; Gerdjikov et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2013; Petersen, 2014; Sreenivasan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: vM1 inputs can convey a simple 'attentional cue' to prepare vS1 barrel cortex neurons for the incoming sensory information from the vibrissae.
source: First, vM1 inputs can convey a simple 'attentional cue' to prepare vS1 barrel cortex neurons for the incoming sensory information from the vibrissae.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional role.

claim: Previous studies have shown that increased attention and especially activation of the frontal eye field area increases the sensitivity and specificity of cortical neurons in sensory visual regions to different visual stimuli.
source: Regarding this possibility, it is interesting to note that previous studies have shown that increased attention and especially activation of the frontal eye field area increases the sensitivity and specificity of cortical neurons in sensory visual regions to different visual stimuli (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Noudoost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the visual system, supported by citations.
